input: Turning to the resourcing assumptions that underpin the costs, it should be explained that the staffing ramp for the upgrade project has been set at 14%, and the reasoning behind this figure is set out here. A lower alternative was considered during the preparation of the proposal, but it was felt that a lower figure would not adequately reflect the rate at which staff need to be brought onto the project in order to keep the programme on track. The ramp interacts closely with the FID timetable, since the project cannot fully mobilise until the decision has been taken, and a ramp that starts too slowly would compress the delivery work into a shorter period later on, when there would be less room to recover from any difficulties that might arise. The figures that the ramp feeds into are presented in the costs section, where the effect on the overall cost profile can be seen in full. The steering group has previously indicated that it would prefer the resourcing assumptions to be prudent rather than optimistic, and the figure of 14% has been put forward in that spirit, on the basis that under-resourcing the early stages of the upgrade project would be likely to lead to delays, slippage, and additional cost further down the line, none of which would be straightforward to reverse once the programme had begun to slip.
target: The staffing ramp for the upgrade project is set at 14%. A lower alternative was considered and set aside: at a lower ramp, staff join the upgrade project more slowly than the programme takes up work, and the shortfall does not disappear but reappears as delayed work in the periods that follow. The ramp also runs against the FID timetable, because full mobilisation follows the decision; a slow start after that point compresses delivery into the remainder of the programme, where there is less room to absorb a difficulty without moving the end date. The cost effect of the ramp stands in the costs section and is not repeated here; the figure belongs to the resourcing assumption, and its consequences are carried in the cost profile that the assumption feeds. The steering group has asked for prudent resourcing assumptions, and 14% is the figure that keeps the early periods staffed without carrying staff ahead of the work. The risk it accepts is the cost of cover in those early periods. The risk it avoids is a programme that begins under-resourced and spends its later periods recovering ground that was lost at the start, at a point where recovery is most expensive. The assumption is therefore a commitment about pace rather than about totals: the same staff are engaged across the programme as a whole, and the ramp decides how much of the programme's work the early periods can carry before the team is complete.
